meta.description: Universally pinned on Leonardo, but this exact aphorism sits in no notebook, the Treatise on Painting, or Wikiquote's sourced corpus — only quote sites. Attributed, unverified.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Where the spirit does not work with the hand, there is no art'?
meta.ogDescription: Widely credited to Leonardo da Vinci and true to his philosophy — but no primary source pins the wording, and the Italian 'original' is a back-translation. Attributed, not verified.

answer.label: Attributed to
answer.sourceLine: Universally credited to Leonardo and faithful to his conviction that art unites the mind and the hand — but no notebook, letter, or the &lgr;compiled Treatise on Painting is known to contain this exact wording. It circulates only on quotation sites, and its Italian ‘original’ appears to be a back-translation of the English, so the phrasing is best treated as attributed rather than verified.

author.name: Leonardo da Vinci
author.heading: About Leonardo da Vinci
author.bio: Leonardo da Vinci was the archetypal Renaissance polymath — painter of the Mona Lisa and The Last Supper, anatomist, engineer, and tireless notebook-keeper. He argued repeatedly that painting is a cosa mentale, an intellectual act in which the disciplined hand serves a seeing mind — which is exactly why aphorisms about spirit, hand, and art attach so easily to his name. His thousands of surviving manuscript pages are also why a genuine line can usually be located, and this one cannot.

cite.sourceCitation: No documented primary source. Earliest attestations are modern quotation collections crediting the line to Leonardo da Vinci; the phrase is absent from Wikiquote's sourced corpus and from the Rigaud translation of Leonardo da Vinci, A Treatise on Painting.

misattribution.heading: Widely quoted, nowhere sourced
misattribution.intro: This is a ‘magnet’ attribution: a polished, uplifting line about art pinned on the era’s most quotable name. It is not known to be wrong — there is no rival author and it fits Leonardo’s outlook — but it is also not verified.

items.why: The sentence is served up by BrainyQuote, Goodreads, AZQuotes and quotefancy with no source, and does not appear in the Treatise on Painting or in Wikiquote’s sourced corpus.

Versions like “Dove lo spirito non lavora con la mano, non c’è arte” and “Quando lo spirito non collabora con le mani…” vary word-for-word with the English and cite no manuscript — the hallmark of a phrase translated back into Italian rather than quoted from Leonardo.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest verdict: credibly Leonardo in spirit, but unproven in the letter — no notebook, letter, or the documented corpus is known to contain this exact sentence.

context.heading: Why it sticks to Leonardo
lead: The line endures because it compresses something Leonardo genuinely believed. Across his writings on painting he insists the craft is a cosa mentale — a thing of the mind — in which manual skill is worthless unless a reasoning, seeing intellect directs it. An aphorism marrying ‘spirit’ and ‘hand’ therefore feels unmistakably his.

That very fit is the trap. Because the sentiment is authentic, few readers pause to ask whether the sentence is; it is repeated as a caption on prints and studio walls without anyone pointing to a page. The idea is well-sourced in Leonardo; this particular formulation is not.
context.pull: Authentic in spirit, unverified in the letter.
